title: How to Increase Humidity in Your House
h1: How Do You Increase Humidity in a Dry House?
description: Dry skin, static shocks and scratchy throats mean your indoor air is too dry. Learn simple ways to add moisture and when a whole-home humidifier makes sense.
quick_answer: For a quick fix, run a portable humidifier in the rooms you use most, and add moisture through everyday habits like air-drying laundry or leaving bath water to cool. For steady, whole-house control, a humidifier installed on your HVAC system adds moisture to all the air it moves. Aim for roughly 30 to 50 percent.
body:
Most of the year, Southern California homes aren't short on moisture, especially near the coast. But when Santa Ana winds blow in from the desert, humidity can drop fast, and inland homes can feel bone dry for days. Running the heater on cold nights dries things out too.

How do you know your house is too dry?

Dry air shows up in your body and in your house:

  • Dry, itchy skin and chapped lips
  • Scratchy throat or nosebleeds, especially in the morning
  • Static shocks when you touch doorknobs
  • Gaps in wood floors or trim, or furniture joints loosening
  • Houseplants drying out faster than usual

A simple digital hygrometer tells you the actual number. Below about 30 percent most people start to feel it.

What are quick ways to add humidity?

For short dry spells, everyday habits add a surprising amount of moisture:

  1. Run a portable humidifier in the bedroom overnight. Use distilled water if your tap water is hard, which much of San Diego County's is, to avoid white mineral dust.
  2. Air-dry laundry on a rack indoors.
  3. Leave bath water in the tub until it cools before draining.
  4. Cook on the stovetop with lids off when it's safe to do so.
  5. Keep the bathroom door open after a shower so the steam spreads.
  6. Add houseplants, which release a little moisture as you water them.

Clean portable humidifiers every few days. Standing water in a dirty tank grows bacteria and mold, which you then breathe in.

Does a whole-home humidifier make sense here?

For many homes, a portable unit is enough. A whole-home humidifier makes more sense if:

  • You live inland where dry Santa Ana days are frequent
  • Someone in the house has asthma, sinus problems or very dry skin
  • You have wood floors, instruments or furniture you want to protect
  • You'd rather not refill and clean portable units every day

A whole-home unit connects to your furnace or air handler and a water line, and adds moisture to the air as it moves through the ducts. It's controlled by a humidistat, so it only runs when the house needs it. There are a few types, including bypass, fan-powered and steam units, and the right one depends on your system and how much moisture you need.

Our indoor air quality team can tell you whether your home is a good fit and size the unit to the house.

Whole-home units need a little care too. Most have a water panel or pad that should be replaced once a year, and the drain line needs to stay clear. We check both during a regular maintenance visit.

Can you add too much humidity?

Yes. Over about 50 to 60 percent, you start to see condensation on windows, musty smells and a higher risk of mold and dust mites. That's a common problem in coastal homes even without a humidifier.

Keep an eye on your hygrometer, and turn the humidifier down if windows fog up on cool mornings. If your home swings between very dry and very damp depending on the weather, whole-home control with a humidistat keeps it steady.

What else helps a dry house?

Air leaks matter. Dry outside air sneaking in through gaps around doors, windows and the attic replaces the moist air you're trying to keep. Weatherstripping and air sealing make any humidifier work better. Your thermostat matters too. Keeping the heat a couple of degrees lower on cold nights dries the air less.

Inland versus coastal homes

Where you live in the county changes the picture. A home a mile from the beach may rarely need added moisture and is more likely to fight dampness. A home in the inland valleys or foothills can swing from comfortable to very dry in a single afternoon when the wind shifts. If you're inland and the dry spells keep coming back each fall and winter, that's when a permanent solution starts to make sense. If you're near the coast, a small portable unit for the occasional Santa Ana stretch is usually plenty.
faqs: What's the ideal indoor humidity level?
Most homes are comfortable at about 30 to 50 percent. Below 30 percent people notice dry skin and static, and above 50 to 60 percent mold and dust mites become more of a concern.
Is it safe to sleep with a humidifier running?
Yes, as long as the unit is clean and the room doesn't get too humid. Clean the tank every few days, use distilled water if you have hard water, and check that windows aren't fogging up.
Not when they're sized and set correctly. A humidistat keeps moisture in a safe range. Problems usually come from settings that are too high or a unit that isn't maintained.
Why is my house so dry during Santa Ana winds?
Santa Ana winds come from the desert and carry very dry air. Every gap in your home lets that air in, and indoor humidity drops quickly, especially in inland areas.
